speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, October 31, 1983, consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motion No. 58 (Mr. McKnight).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Before we proceed with further consideration of the Bill at report stage, I would like to refer to the motions placed on the Notice Paper last Monday with the unanimous consent of the House.
As Hon. Members are aware, a great many of these motions were previously ruled out of order on procedural grounds. It is not the intention of the Chair to interfere with the unanimous agreement of the House to place the motions back on the Notice Paper for consideration. However, even though the House has agreed to set aside its rules and practices in some regards and go beyond any procedural limitations in regard to these motions, the Chair is still confronted with a major difficulty.
Eight of the motions involve the additional expenditure of public funds and, therefore, require a Royal Recommendation which can only be signed by His Excellency. The four motions standing in the name of the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy), namely Motions Nos. 14A, 74A, 157A and 160A, have been covered by the required Royal Recommendations. However, Motions Nos. 51 A, 125A, 126A and 157A, standing in the names of the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong), the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko), the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) respectively, are not so accompanied.
Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Citation 543(1), provides:
If any motion or bill or proceeding is offered to be moved, whether in the House or in a committee which requires, but fails to receive, the recommendation of the Crown, it is the duty of the Speaker to announce that no question can be proposed upon the motion, or to direct the withdrawal of the bill, or to say that the problem may be rectified by the proposer obtaining a Royal Recommendation.
The citation is clear and unequivocal and is backed by long practice. Under the circumstances and in light of this citation, I do not see how 1 can in conscience, respecting my obligations to the House, accept that Motions Nos. 51 A, 125A, 126A and 157B can be proposed for consideration. No unanimous consent can get around the problem. I regret very much that I have to reach this decision, but 1 hope all Hon. Members will appreciate the difficult position in which the Chair has been placed.
1 would also like to indicate to the House that the motions placed on the Notice Paper by unanimous consent on Monday last have been inserted in their proper numerical order and given, as the case may be, a letter A or B, in addition to an arabic numeral, so that all those motions which have been before us would not need to be renumbered. The new motions are Motions Nos. 10A, 14A, 74A, 90A, 134A, 154A, 157A, 160A, 165A and 165B.
Once consideration of Motion No. 58 now before the House is completed, the next motion to be considered will be Motion No. 10A. It in turn will be followed by debate on Motion No. 14A. Both will also be voted on separately. Motions Nos. 157A and 74A ought to be debated together. Since Motion No. 74A is consequential to Motion No. 157A, a vote on Motion No. 157A would also dispose of Motion No. 74A. Motion No. 90A should be debated and voted on separately.
Motion No. 134A will be grouped for debate with previously grouped Motions Nos. 63, 68, 69, 99 to 103 inclusive, 115, 127, 128, 130 to 133 inclusive, 136 to 138 inclusive, 140 to 144 inclusive, 148 and 149. An affirmative vote on Motion No. 133 will dispose of Motion No. 134A; however, a negative vote on Motion No. 133 would necessitate the question being put on Motion No. 134A.
Motion No. 160A should be grouped with the previous grouping of Motions Nos. 159, 160, 161 and 162 for debate, which had been grouped for debate but separate votes. It is my intention to group Motions Nos. 160A and 160 for voting as follows: An affirmative vote on Motion No. 160A negates the need for putting the question on Motion No. 160, while a negative vote on Motion No. 160A would require the putting of the question on Motion No. 160.
Motion No. 154A will be grouped for debate with the previously grouped Motions Nos. 153 and 154, and each will be voted on separately.
Motions Nos. 165A and 165B ought to be grouped for debate and an affirmative vote on Motion No. 165A will dispose of Motion No. 165B; however, a negative vote on Motion No. 165A would require the putting of the question on

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, might 1 just interject, not for the purpose of coming to the rescue of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), but merely to make an observation without in any way reflecting on the ruling of the Chair. There has been a practice that has grown up in the House which I, and I am sure all Members, would like to see retained in situations such as the one which the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain is attempting to speak to today and which by our custom he is prevented from doing.
Normally the occupant of the chair, as Madam Speaker did when these amendments had to be dealt with, generally expresses concern about the acceptability of a motion or motions and warns Members that the Chair does have concern and will hear submissions at some later time. I am in accord with the Chair, so naturally I cannot question it. However, I would suggest that we would not want to dispense with that past practice and replace it with the practice where the Speaker initiates rulings without any warning to Members who may wish to make some submissions in the future.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has made an observation which the Chair will heed carefully. The Chair, however, has considered this matter, taken advice and is firmly of the opinion as expressed.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to remind the House of Standing Order 79(10), which provides, and I quote:
(10) The Speaker shall have power to select or combine amendments or clauses to be proposed at the report stage and may, if he or she thinks fit, call upon any Member who has given notice of an amendment to give such explanation of the subject of the amendment as may enable the Speaker to form a judgment upon it.
It is clear that in this case, the Chair did not think it would be useful to exercise its discretionary powers and call upon a Member to explain the subject of the amendment. The Chair made its ruling without consulting the Hon. Member, and I think this is sound practice because it saves considerable time. Not long ago, this latitude was still granted, and the result was that precious time was wasted in the House of Commons, and I think that the Chair now tends to simply apply the Standing Order. I realize that the Standing Orders are seldom crystal clear, but I must say I welcome this return to strict application of the Standing Orders, as opposed to a not so literal interpretation when the Standing Orders are clear and allowing any number of interventions, as has been the case in the past, unfortunately, which has led to considerable waste of time.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that notwithstanding the Chair's ruling, which I respect, if there is a way to allow the House to give its unanimous consent for a vote on the amendments that were rejected this morning-I realize that the Chair, in giving its ruling, explained that it was difficult, but nevertheless the Chair reiterated that on this side of the House, we would give that unanimous consent if it was required and if it would allow the Chair to put the question on these amendments. However, without wishing to oppose the Chair's ruling, I want to make it quite clear that this is not a case of obstruction or opposition on the part of the Government. The Chair's ruling is there, and we respect it, but if unanimous consent would be useful for the New Democratic Party, we are prepared to give it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Chair is in a difficult position. The Chair has considered the matter of the Royal Recommendation, a long-standing practice of the House. Motions that require a Royal Recommendation and do not have a Royal Recommendation cannot be put before the House. The Chair has not been able to overcome this very great difficulty, in fact insuperable difficulty, with regard to procedural acceptability of motions. If there is unanimous agreement of the House Leaders to put some type of motion or amendment before the House, the Chair at this stage can only suggest that there might be consultations and it might be possible for the House Leaders to come back with further suggestions. The Chair is the servant of the House, but at this stage the Chair cannot see its way to accepting motions that clearly require a Royal Recommendation, which is not there for those four amend-
November 3, 1983

merits. With regret, because of the unanimous decision of the House, the Chair has had to make the ruling that it has made and the Chair does not do this lightly.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in a bit of a quandary because we understood when we agreed to give unanimous consent to allow certain matters to be put on the Notice Paper and voted upon that we likewise were being given unanimous consent for that practice to be followed in the case of the amendments we put in. We had no indication from anyone at the time that there would be a counter-ruling made which would result in our not being permitted to vote on our amendments. I must say that had that matter been made clear to us at the start we would not have acceded to the unanimous consent being given on the other questions.
1 want to suggest that there is perhaps a way out. The unanimous consent was given, 1 believe, by both sides of the House with the understanding that the questions would be put to a vote. 1 would like the Chair simply to consider whether or not in the circumstances, given that the Hosue is entitled to give unanimous consent to a matter such as this, and without establishing a precedent, as is clearly set out in Citation 14 of Beauchesne, that the intent of the House would be thwarted if the vote were not allowed to be taken.
1 can appreciate the difficulty of the Royal Recommendation. I would like to suggest that what we are offering in at least two of the three amendments can be considered as amendments to the Government proposal which has, in fact, a Royal Recommendation. The Government has put forward a proposal on the question of shipper share under 157A, and in the normal process of debate we would have been able to offer an amendment to that proposal as long as our amendment did not require the Government to spend more money than they had heretofore allocated for 157A.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Chair is listening to the Hon. Member and is seeking a way out of the difficulty. All the Chair can suggest at this point is that there might be some conversations between House Leaders of the Parties to see whether amendments can be offered in a form which would come within the scope of the Royal Recommendation. It appears from what the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain is saying that there might be a disposition on the part of the Government to make amendments to the legislation so that matters might be so considered.
The Chair has a problem with the Royal Recommendation. The precedents are abundantly clear. It is one of those things that the Chair cannot set aside.
The Chair would like to suggest that the House Leaders, especially the House Leader for the Government and the House Leader for the New Democratic Party, have a private conference and see whether it is possible to frame amendments in such a way that they can be brought within the scope.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is very important to make sure that the record is clear. There are two points to be
Western Grain Transportation Act
made. First, we did hold discussions concerning the acceptance of amendments for debate, and the position we took was that if Members of the Opposition Parties wanted to bring such amendments forward, we would not object. I think it is important to point out to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) that in the discussion we did not receive copies of their proposed amendments until minutes before Question Period-almost minutes before consent was to be given. We had no opportunity to determine their advisability within the scope of what is normally considered the Royal Recommendation. I believe that that is within the discretion of the Chair. The offer was made and accepted but because there was no time to give them a full examination and make that judgment, I do not think we can be held responsible.
Second, let us make it clear that there is no disposition on the part of the Government to accept such amendments. We are prepared to have them debated but I want to make it clear we are not prepared to have them accepted. If they want to debate them, that is well and good. But if you are suggesting that we try to rework them so that they are acceptable, 1 think you will find that negotiations would not lead very far.
Mr. Speaker, I want to carry on with the debate on the motion put by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight).

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. 1 thought we were still debating this point of order but since my hon. colleague is entering into debate-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the Hon. Member, there is no further debate on the point of order; the matter has been settled. The Hon. Member is recognized for debate.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on another point of order.

All 1 want to say, Mr. Speaker, is that you made a ruling this morning, we are abiding by that ruling and we can live with it. However, since you suggested that 1 have some discussions with the New Democratic Party's House Leader, if the Chair is not advised of any unanimous consent in the course of the day, the Chair's ruling stands and we shall vote on the amendments as the Chair ruled, and I want that to be quite clear.
In other words, I would not want your suggestion for consultations to be an excuse for delaying the vote until later this evening. 1 want to make that quite clear.

Mr. Speaker, I want to return to the merits of the debate. At the outset of today, the last day of report stage because of the invocation of closure by the Government, I think it is important that we spend time debating the issue.
The Government House Leader mentioned that there have been delays on points of order. I suggest that the ultimate

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
delay was caused by the Minister himself when he had the audacity to move the adjournment of debate at 4.30 on Tuesday morning. At that time, Members on this side of the House were quite prepared to continue debating on our own time, regardless of whether we got any sleep, because we believe this is an important issue. The Minister was embarrassed and ashamed of the position of the Government on this issue and so moved the adjournment. This caused him to lose the ability to put this matter through before the Armistice Day break. I know that Members of the Liberal Party are seething and unhappy over the incompetence of the Minister in the way in which he did this. I simply would like on one occasion to join with Liberal backbenchers and say that I am mad as hell about this and so is everybody on our side.
[DOT] (U25)
This particular proposal, which was put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), is a very sensible one. Before the Minister moved the adjournment of the House at 4.30 a.m. on Tuesday, he said he was going to take this matter under advisement but he did not think that any of his legal advisers were up at that time. He wanted to adjourn the House so he could get competent legal advice with respect to the admissibility of this very sensible motion. The Minister has had all of Tuesday morning, all day Wednesday, and all of this morning to consult with his legal counsel to find out whether or not this particular provision can in fact be accepted by the Government. I will be anxious to hear, now that the Minister has had three days to consider the matter, whether this motion will be accepted.
This motion proposes to specify that in fact the railways will be held under obligation to provide suitable accommodation for grain. This is a matter of some serious consequence because the whole proposal which the Government has brought forward is an extremely rich package as far as the railways of Canada are concerned. 1 said on an earlier occasion that if 1 were on the board of directors of CPR 1 would commission a statue of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) and have those statues put in the foyer of the headquarters of the CPR, because the CPR is really beholden to the Government for this rich package. 1 can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the people of western Canada understand that. When they are called upon to pay an enormous price in terms of extra cost to move their grain, they will not forget what the Liberal Party has done to them with this legislation.
Another point made by my colleague, which I believe is very helpful, is that under this provision the Administrator of the transportation agency is deemed to be a shipper for purposes of making an application, which would be at public expense but on behalf of the producers, with respect to any inability on the part of the railways to carry the grain of the western producers. 1 believe this is a very sensible proposition because what is going to happen, under the circumstances we now have in this Bill, is that if there is any complaint, the individual producer, either himself or in co-operation with his fellow farmers, will at his own expenses have to petition with respect
to inequities which may in fact occur as a result of the inability of the railways to carry out their mandate and obligation to move the grain to export points.
1 also want to voice my concern that one of the motions which has been proposed by the New Democratic Party has in fact been ruled out of order. The reason I am sorry that this motion was not brought up for a vote on the floor of the House is that it is a motion which, in my estimation, demonstrates the greatest turnaround by any political party in recent history. With respect to the motion brought forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster, in regard to assisting the movement of grain and making sure the railways carry out their obligations, the New Democratic Party has now done a great flip-flop in its attitude toward the retention of the statutory Crow rate. The implication is clear from the motion it put forward that the New Democratic Party, as my colleague the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has said, has now taken the position that the Crow must go. It has done a complete 180 degree reversal over the position they ostensibly took.
Do you believe that?

As you can see, Mr. Speaker, 1 have two pieces of paper. One is the motion put forward by the Minister of Transport with respect to the safety net provisions. The other one, Mr. Speaker, is an NDP amendment. You can see from your chair that these two documents are typed on the same typewriter. They are precisely the same with one exception; they blotted out a part of the safety net provision and inserted their own figures. Instead of the Government provision of 4 per cent in 1984, 5 per cent in 1985, 8 per cent in 1986, 9 per cent in 1987 and 10 per cent after 1988, they put in their own provision of 3 per cent.
It must be a mistake.

No mistake, Mr. Speaker. As I said, they did not have the grace to use their own typewriter; they used a Government typewriter and put in exactly the same motion. What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? It means the NDP has flip-flopped.

I point out that there is nothing more relevant to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster, which requires the CTC to ensure the railways carry out their obligation to provide adequate accommodation for the movement of grain. What are they going to consider? They will consider the cost to the railways and their level of payment. Therefore, we have then to assess how much should the railways be paid. Their motion, whether it was ruled out of order or not, deals specifically with that very question. Therefore it is of the highest relevance.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain raised a point of order and he is correct in that at some time during the remarks of the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West considerable reference was made to a motion ruled out of order. I think the proper route for me is to suggest the Hon. Member try to address himself to Motion No. 58 and try to contain his remarks in that regard.

You have a record of fairness and equity in this matter, Mr. Speaker, and as you know I always follow your rulings with absolute dedication. I propose to do just that. All I can say with respect to the position of the NDP-I am not going to refer to any particular motion ruled out of order so I will not be irrelevant-is that their position, generally speaking, and having no regard to motions ruled out of order, is that they have done a flip-flop on how much the railways should in fact receive for the movement of grain. These people are absolutely shameless.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, my understanding of the rules of order in this House is that Members in debate cannot impute motives to individual Members or Parties.

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: 1 think the Hon. Member has done this by a total misinterpretation of something of which he apparently knows very little. If I may explain-
No.
Try and explain it during the election.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) should seek the floor in debate if he wishes to explain something. With respect to the point of order, the Hon. Member is correct but I think the Chair has a duty to allow as wide ranging a debate as possible. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon West has only four minutes approximately remaining. If he could be allowed to continue his remarks we can move on to less rambunctious debate.
Western Grain Transportation Act

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the NDP is so sensitive over this terribly bad policy they have adopted. Imagine how you would feel if you had gone around telling the people of western Canada that you want to retain the Crow and the first chance you have to do anything with respect to this legislation is to give the western farmers a hick in the slats to the extent of a 20 per cent increase right now in the cost of transporting grain. You would be livid, Mr. Speaker, and 1 see you understand that.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we in this Party have taken a firm and consistent position with respect to the retention of the Crow. The freeze is an understandable, fair and reasonable position for our Party to take with respect to this matter until after the review period has been completed.
What do I mean by that? We say out west you do not want to buy a pig in a poke. They say that out east as well, and 1 am going to say it right here in central Canada. We do not want to buy a pig in a poke. We want to see how this system operates. Would you buy a bill of goods, Mr. Speaker, and pay for it before you see whether it works, without any guarantees? Not on your life. But that is what the grain producer is asked to accept. There are all sorts of vague references to the obligations of the railways, all sorts of talk about safety nets, but in the final result the NDP and the Liberals are saying the farmers pay more without seeing whether or not this system is going to work. Well, we say the western farmer does not deserve that kind of contemptuous action on the part of the Government.
My colleague from Kindersley-Lloydminster, along with Members of our Party, attended faithfully all the hearings on this matter in committee. Where were the NDP Members? Where were these defenders of the Crow? Except for the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre who were there half the time, the rest of them were there on one or two occasions to get their pictures taken. This was so that they would have a photograph to send out in their householder mailing.
People in our Party hold permits and know what it is to get on the land and produce. They know the problem involved in grain transportation. My colleague makes a proposal which is going to put an additional and specific obligation on the part of the railways to deliver, and I cannot understand why anyone in this House would not support this wholeheartedly.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Minister, before he moved adjournment of the House, indicated he was sympathetic to this matter. 1 think it would be incumbent upon him or his Parliamentary Secretary to let us know whether or not we are going to have this proposal added to the Bill. Opposing as we do the ruinous aspect of this legislation, we have tried to be constructive in this debate. We have attempted to say that we object to this legislation but here are some things the Government should consider. I hope the Minister will give fair and sympathetic consideration to putting in this very useful

Western Grain Transportation Act
amendment and I look forward to someone from the Government standing up and accepting our proposition.

We were advised in committee that there was no need for Motion No. 58. We

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak on Motion No. 58 which presents a long and detailed regurgitation of a lot of what is now in the Transportation Act. It attempts simply to restate some of those clauses

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
into this Bill. I do not know whether there is very much to be said about this long and detailed amendment except that it contains a lot of words that are already written into law and are part of the current Transportation Act. It really changes very little or changes nothing. It simply goes over many things that are now in existing laws. It simply transfers some phrases into this Bill.
For instance, the first aspect of the motion talks about furnishing adequate and suitable accommodation for the receiving and loading of grain offered for carriage upon the railroad. This would normally mean new sidings. That has been part of the Railway Act for many years. It has been written into law that the railways must provide the sidings. But in actual fact if a customer wants a siding, for the past number of years the customer has had to pay for it. That has been written into this Bill, but it is already in other laws. Therefore, it will not change anything. I submit that it will only reiterate present laws that are not being enforced.
This motion also goes on to say that it would furnish adequate and suitable accommodation for the carrying, unloading and delivering of grain. That sounds like hopper and railway cars. Yet we know for a fact that in spite of this being part of the existing Railway Act, no cars have been purchased by either railway company for the movement of grain since the 1950s.
In subparagraph (c) we read:
(c)	without delay, and with due care and diligence, receive, carry and deliver all such grain;
That provision is already in the Railway Act. It is a very detailed piece of legislation, yet we know that in 1977-1978 the CPR refused to supply cars to move grain and the Wheat Board and the Provinces ended up having to buy cars to get the grain moving again.
Motion No. 58 subparagraph (d) reads:
(d)	furnish and use all proper appliances, accommodation and means necessary for receiving, loading, carrying, unloading and delivering such grain;
One would think that would include up to and including branch lines. We know that in spite of this being a part of existing transportation law, and having a branch line act providing subsidies to provide service on those branch lines, the branch lines are not being maintained, even those that have been designated to be kept up by the Canadian Transport Commission. We know the cost of upgrading them to meet CTC rulings is something like $1.6 billion. The Government has only $1.1 billion to put toward that objective and the railways are refusing to find the other half billion.
We know these things are not happening in spite of all these fine things in Motion No. 58 that already exist in laws and apply to the railway system. We see that there are sections on due payment of tolls lawfully imposed by the Act. We see there are portions in here that deal with payments. There is a section dealing with how persons who are aggrieved by the railways under this act may act against the companies for the refusal of the company to comply with the requirements of this section. It is almost a straight removal of a similar section in
the Railway Act that exists now. We know that was not successfully used. It is not something farmers can use. Farmers did take the CPR and the CNR to court because of their refusal to provide adequate rolling stock and service in 19771978. The courts ruled that the law was not strong enough. The court said the farmers were not in law the shipper and could therefore not act against the railway. These fine words being lifted out of a couple of other acts and put into this one will not change the way the system operates.
I would like to say a few words about the producers' share of costs in this Bill. It seems to me there is not a current way of protecting farmers from paying more than a specified share of the cost of freight. That is why there has been a discussion about 3 per cent or 7 per cent or 10 per cent.
1 would like to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that over the past number of years the shipper's share of the freight charges on the six major grains, according to figures put out by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, has been as follows. In the 19791980 crop year the average percentage of the price of the shippers' share was 3 per cent. In 1980-1981 the average share of the freight for the six major grains was 2.6 per cent. In the 1981-1982 crop year the shippers' share was 3 per cent. The shippers' share is not quite the same thing as the safety net, but I put in these figures so you can compare them with the proposal for the safety net to show how relevant the figures are, Mr. Speaker.
The safety net is a ceiling that would provide a net above which-
It is 2.5 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
-the proportion of freight costs cannot climb. I have just read into the record how it has been 3 per cent for the last couple of crop years and that it dropped to 2.6 per cent in 1980-1981 essentially because the price of the grain went up in 1980-1981. That is the secret. If the price of grain continues to fall along the line that it started back in June, 3 per cent would be a safety net even under the current rate.
If the Conservatives could do arithmetic or had any analytical ability, they would know, even under the current rate which is what we have been talking about all through this debate, that if the price of grain goes below $1.50 per tonne for the six grains on a weighted average, there would be more than 3 per cent of the producers' income going to pay freight even under the current Crow rate. A 3 per cent safety net guarantees producers against additional freight costs even with the existing Crow rate. That is a fact that some of my colleagues on this side of the House totally ignore. They are completely ignorant of facts. They do not wish to read, listen or understand. While we hear a lot of them saying they are farmers, that they have quota books and their understanding of this issue is all knowing and supreme because of this fact, they, I think, are kidding themselves. They are attempting to fool the Canadian people, but they are only fooling themselves.

With the 3 per cent safety net which I have proposed, when the price of grain falls a little more, as has been the case in the last few months, the actual Crow rate would be forced down.
Since this matter has been raised six or seven times by Hon. Members of the Conservative Party, I think it is time the true facts on the safety net were presented. I hope it is debated from here on in on the basis of the actual facts instead of illogical falsehoods.

However, what the Government has overlooked and what many of these witnesses have overlooked is the effect that Bill C-155 has on the producer, because the producer in western Canada is the one most affected by the change. I was surprised that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) should make a comment regarding the fact that a number of Members on this side of the House were in conflict of interest because they held permit books. speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Dubois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in the debate on Bill C-155 and more specifically on Motion No. 58 before the House today.
1 must say 1 find the Motion situation-we have now had over 80 motions-rather surprising after sitting on the Transport Committee and conducting hearings across the country, and subsequently considering the Bill, clause by clause, in late August and all through September-and seeing a situation where motions were submitted to the Committee by the Official Opposition to reduce the number of members on the administrating Committee and today, another motion is being proposed to have the same number we had in the Bill originally. As for Motion No. 58, when questions were asked during clause by clause consideration in committee, the legal expert said at the time that this provision already existed in the Railway Act.
I am rather surprised at the whole situation, because to me, Mr. Speaker, this is just filibustering, and has definitely no connection with the aspirations of Canadians, not even those of Western Canada. 1 heard the previous speaker saying that no one on this side of the House understood the producers, and 1 would like to remind him that when we were conducting hearings in Regina, his hometown, the chairman of the Prairie Farm Commodity Coalition, when asked whether producers were able to pay more, answered yes, and of course, there were many members of the National Farmers Union in the room at the time in Regina who did not entirely agree. But 1 think that the Prairie Farm Commodity Coalition is a very farsighted group that sees the future of Western agriculture in a different perspective, and it was, in fact, Mr. McMillan who said at the time that producers were able to pay more.
As for the motion before the House today, namely Motion No. 58 which concerns Clause 33, and considering what we were told by Mr. Lefebvre in his answer to a number of questions, 1 feel, Mr. Speaker, that this motion is merely being added to the number of motions we already have to add to the delay, just like the four positions of the Progressive Conservative Party, and perhaps I may explain. It has become their trademark to put motions like the one before the House today to make people think they are very concerned, when in fact, they are merely trying to play for time or to waste time, because, Mr. Speaker, since I chaired a sub-committee in the

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act Quebec caucus on this issue. 1 remember clearly that in March, the Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) said in the House, when the motion was being proposed, that the Liberal Members who had formed the sub-committee should persuade the Government to change the method of payment and that it was intolerable. He even wanted us to resign. At the time, the Member for Joliette was referring to payments to the railways and not to producers. Then all of a sudden we heard their official critic talking about freedom of choice. This option, and even Motion No. 58, are issues we discussed with representatives of the agricultural industry in Quebec, to find out what they thought. Well, the answer we got when we conducted hearings in Quebec was that the concept of freedom of choice was the ultimate in hypocritical posturing, and that was the position defended by the Progressive Conservative Party.
1 would like to comment on another position defended by the Progressive Conservative Party and a statement was reported in the newspaper La Terre de chez nous, referring to the leadership campaign when the present leader was still just a candidate he said in Alberta that he was going to help producers and if possible direct payments to producers. That was the third position taken by the Progressive Conservative Party. And finally, they managed to come up with a fourth position when they talked about maintaining the status quo, and this is because Official Opposition does not know where it is going and is really ambivalent about the issue, because when we were in the Vancouver area and people came to our hearings, they said: to do nothing would be the worst that could happen. Something must be done about the very substantial investments expected in the Vancouver area. Local Members who were there-some were not-and even some Members of the New Democratic Party came to our hearings, and that is where they heard from the local mayors. Some of them were more or less told off and even Members of the Official Opposition were told that the worst that could happen in connection with the Bill and investments to be made in the Vancouver area by CN and CP, if the Bill was not passed, doing nothing would be the worst that could happen. So I feel that as the Government we must make a choice, and consider what is important for breeders and producers, and in this connection, we must not forget that under Clause 59, we are establishing a committee to review the operation of this legislation and the effectiveness of the method of payment, and to examine the implications. We met members of the Prairie Farm Commodity Coalition, and of course they had some apprehension, but this is a solution that is attractive to them and they are in favour of being able to examine the implications and having a committee consisting of at least three and not more than five members and reporting before March 1985, to inform the Department about what is going on.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that in view of the situation and the large scale investments expected both in Western and Eastern Canada, including the manufacturing of hopper cars and
railroad tracks, and prospective investments in the Vancouver terminal area, to create jobs in an area which, as the House knows, is suffering from some disruption at the present time, that is why a group of mayors came to give us their point of view.
1 believe that we must not stop this process and that we must therefore see to it that the bill is passed. Unfortunately, because of the obstructive methods used by the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party, we have been forced to set a limit on the number of days for the debate. Normally, Mr. Speaker, the Committee was to report to the House on September 12. However, there were many discussions in committee and the Opposition members said: "We may not be able to do it by September 12; we shall perhaps need a few more days." We trusted them and granted a few more days to discuss this bill. However, it was a futile exercise because, when we were able to report to the House, there was still more obstruction in spite of the fact that during the committee hearings, we had heard all possible viewpoints about this bill and absolutely everyone was heard.
I even recall one day in Regina when our hearings began at 9 o'clock. We did not stop for lunch or dinner. We heard all the groups and even individual witnesses until 10:30 or 1 1 that evening. Committee members on both sides organized a rotation. We heard all the witnesses. It has been said that producers cannot pay more, but some of them at least tell us that they can. What they fear is the effect on livestock producers and the possibility of these producers being hurt by this bill.
As for the livestock producers, they are the ones who asked the government to change not this bill, but this situation because of the problems involved. They are asking however that the payment be made to producers on the basis of acreage.
There had been the Gilson report. Then, there was the 50/50 formula and another proposal for a middle-of-the-road solution. This is why now with this bill, Mr. Speaker, we must make the payment to the railways because it is a transportation problem, and afterwards look at the effects of this change in committee.
It is not what the Progressive Conservatives and the NDP want. So far the Progressive Conservatives have had four positions. They are all mixed up because they have to say something in Quebec and something else in Western Canada, so that they will not lose any votes. That is in fact their position. As for the New Democratic Party, their position is to do absolutely nothing, to maintain the status quo, in spite of everything that the progressive groups in Western Canada want.
We should therefore pass this bill and implement it. Then, when the Committee submits its report in 1985, people in Western and Eastern Canada will know what are its final consequences, and if it is necessary to make adjustments to improve the situation, the Government can make them, but

Mr. Speaker, the Government proposes to cancel the special tax advantages available to people working and living in the North despite the protests of every group with any understanding of development in that area, including some parts of the Government itself.
The cancellation of these northern benefits will bring in only a small amount of additional revenue to the Finance Department and have a disastrous effect on industries such as mining. Instead, it will simply add employees of large companies and Governments to the list of people suffering these disadvantages.
We on this side of the House can find only one explanation for the decision, and that is that the Government intends to replace a stimulant available to all, with a grant system available only to those it selects. This has been the pattern of economic assistance over the last several years, and it is one with grave consequences. Industry spokesmen have pointed out that the grant system rewards industries whose imminent failure means political problems for the Government. They have said the grant system is "addictive", and that it forces bureaucrats to make decisions about the validity of industrial efforts with which they may not be familiar.
It is time the effort was made to provide stimulative tax measures for everyone, so that personal and industrial initiative can take advantage of opportunities instead of turning to the Government and asking for a special grant or loan.

subtopic: RESTRICTIONS ON TRANSPORTATION OF HAY TO UNITED STATES
RESTRICTIONS ON TRANSPORTATION OF HAY TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to bring attention to a situation which is causing concern to a number of Canadians, many of whom reside in my constituency of Fraser Valley East and other areas on the Province of British Columbia. I am speaking of the problem of reciprocity in the treatment of truck drivers between Canada and the United States.
The situation has been ongoing for a number of years, but on June 1, 1983, the Canadian hay dealers were notified that they no longer would be allowed to take unloading crews into the United States. While the order in itself does not constitute a serious limitation to hay movement if the situation is handled the same on both sides of the border, the enforcement has been much more prohibitive in the United States than in Canada. United States drivers continue to assist in the unloading of hay imported into Canada from the U.S.A. by United States dealers.
As there are some 4,000 instances of hay importation from the United States to Canada, and as U.S. alfalfa hay will remain in demand for our high producing dairy herds in British Columbia for many years to come, we urge that customs officials take measures to ensure that equal treatment is accorded to Canadian hay dealers to permit them to compete in their own marketplace.
As well, there is concern that loads of hay are not moving directly from the U.S. to the farms which have bought the hay.
In some cases U.S. hay dealers have set up a sales location to use as a base from which to sell hay. Such action constitutes further unfair competition with Canadian hay dealers.

During retirement years an individual's income in the majority of cases will drop dramatically, and many financial adjustments are made necessary. Also, many seniors will discover that for the first time in their lives it has become necessary to pay their income tax by quarterly instalment. This longstanding provision of the Income Tax Act was originally designed to help individuals avoid interest penalties. However, through lack of understanding of the income tax provisions, and because of errors in the calculation of yearly income, many senior citizens are still faced with instalment interest penalties at year end.
While the Department of National Revenue has made an effort to improve the notification process for individuals who are required to pay their income tax by instalments, there is a need for further review and clarification of this provision as it affects senior citizens. It is my hope that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), in reviewing any changes to the Income Tax Act, will give the concerns of Canada's seniors their utmost consideration.

Mr. Speaker, 1 answered a similar question yesterday by the leader of the New Democratic Party. Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture my question is directed to the Minister of State for International Trade. As he is aware, the potato industry in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick is anxiously awaiting the announcement of the U.S. Department of Commerce concerning allegations of the dumping of Maritime potatoes into the New England states. Sales to the United States from the Maritime potato industry have averaged $32 million per year and this is crucial to the economy of the Maritime Provinces. Not only are these financial aspects at stake, but this case will set a precedent for all cases concerning trade with the U.S. in agricultural commodities.
I think the Minister is aware that recently a Bill was introduced in the United States Senate by Senator D'Amato which, if passed, would impose heavy tariffs on all fresh vegetables entering the U.S. from Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege with respect to a disservice I did to
Privilege-Mr. Sargeant
Mr. Ron Atkey, a previous Member of this House and a former Minister. At page 28450 of Hansard for Friday, October 28, 1983, I asked a question of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts). In my supplementary question, I mentioned Mr. Atkey's name. I would like to read just a part of my question as follows:
A number of immigration consultants and lawyers, including the Hon. Minister's predecessor, Ron Atkey, the Conservative Minister, have been to Hong Kong to take advantage of this bonanza business. Does the Minister think that our immigration policy, which favours business investment over family reunification, can lead to inequalities, and encourages these sharks to go to Hong Kong and say that you can in fact buy your way into Canada, at a time when the Hong Kong people are very uneasy over the renewal of the British treaty with China? Is not the policy itself inherently inequitable when it leads to this kind of situation?
It seems to me on rereading Hansard that I was inadvertently classifying Mr. Atkey as a shark. I did not want to do that. I never intended to do that. Mr. Atkey is not a shark. He is a prominent and good lawyer. I have dealt with him in the past.
He has not approached me. 1 read Hansard and I realized that I would be doing a terrible disservice if I left my remarks as they were in Hansard. I tried to clarify the matter outside the House with the press. I kept to the point that I was trying to make in the House that there were rip-offs in Hong Kong and because of the uneasiness there a lot of lawyers, including Mr. Atkey, had flocked to Hong Kong. I did not want to convey the impression and I do not want to convey the impression that Mr. Atkey is in any way a shark. I want to clarify that and to withdraw that remark. I do not think it has caused Mr. Atkey any problem, but if it has I apologize to him.

Mr. Speaker, it is exactly because that report has not been laid before the House that 1 feel my privileges as a Member of this House have been violated. I refer specifically to the report on Indian Self-Gov-

November 3, 1983
Privilege-Mr. Sargeant
ernment, the contents of which have been widely covered in much of today's press.
First 1 shall read Citation 647 of Beauchesne, which states in part:
The publication of proceedings of committees conducted with closed doors or of reports of committees before they are available to Members will, however, constitute a breach of privilege.
Let me elaborate briefly on my personal concern. I consider the subject matter of this report to be of great importance to all Canadian natives. I sat on this committee very briefly last spring and I have been looking forward for some months now to the final report of that Committee.
1 would point out that in my constituency there are 11 reserves. The chiefs of all of these reserves have been following this exercise, this study of self-government, very closely. In recent weeks a number of those chiefs have asked me if they could get copies of this report. 1 had to inform them that the report was confidential until such time as it was tabled in the House. 1 promised to make this report available to them as soon as it was tabled in the House.
1 have been told by our caucus representative on that Committee, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), that the report will not now be tabled until at least November 14.
I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that next week during the break 1 have already scheduled a number of meetings with chiefs in my constituency to discuss any number of concerns. You can well imagine that the first question will be: Why can we not have copies of this report when it is now widely circulated? To say the least, Mr. Speaker, 1 will be a touch embarrassed to have to admit to them that even Members of Parliament cannot get their hands on this report while much of the press have seen it. Given that this report has been so widely covered, 1 am not sure what kind of credibility they will attach to my disclaimer. According to one rumour 1 picked up this morning-I stress it is only a rumour-there are now 150 copies of this report circulating outside the House of Commons. I do not want to be critical at all of the press for the role it has played in this matter. After all, the press was only doing its job in reporting this leak. But I must be critical of some unnamed and indeed unknown member of that Committee- the only possible source of that leak would be somebody on the committee-who showed no concern for the rights and privileges of all Members of this House by leaking the report.
From my own personal point of view, the only possible solution would be for the chairman of that Committee to table that report in this House right now.

I wish very briefly to add my submission with respect to that matter so that it might be considered thoroughly by the Chair before rendering a decision on the question of privilege raised. Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by my constituents who are concerned that the repayment of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation assistance for mortgage pay-

Mr. Speaker, I have the duty and honour to present a petition on behalf of constituents of Fraser Valley West, expressing support for Canada's full participation in the NATO and NORAD alliances and requesting that Canada honour its obligations toward the defence of the free world and take all necessary action, including the testing of the Cruise missile in Canada to achieve these goals. The nature of the petition is to indicate that in the face of Soviet conventional and nuclear military superiority and intransigence in seriously negotiating at the START INF and MBFR talks that unilateral disarmament initiatives would have a destabilizing and regressive effect on the reduction of weapons. The purpose of this petition is, therefore, to support the concept of the balance of power and negotiating from a position of mutual strength as the foundation of pursuing both security and disarmament to lower levels of armaments through mutual balanced and verifiable reductions.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motion No. 58 (Mr. McKnight).
Western Grain Transportation Act

Mr. Speaker, I will try to continue my remarks on the Conservative Motion No. 58. When I was speaking before lunch 1 was interrupted several times.
1 should like to recap some of my comments. 1 was trying to put forward several arguments. First, the Government does not like to listen to opposition, regardless where it comes from. That is an erosion of democracy in the country. Second, there is no difference between the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party. Had the Conservative Party been the Government or should it become the Government, or had the Liberals not tried to force the Bill through-I would remind Hon. Members that it is not through yet-then the Conservative Party would have brought it in. The Conservatives should realize the negative impact of the legislation on many communities along small branch lines in western Canada.
The Conservatives often say that the NDP Members are not very knowledgeable on this subject as not many Members of this Party hold permit books. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that some Members of the New Democratic Party who sit in the House are permit book holders. They know as much about grain transportation as anyone in the House; in fact, in most cases they know more about it.
The Conservative Party has put forth many arguments which do not relate to grain transportation. They have asserted that the NDP does not want the Crow rate to be maintained. I say that we do; we have always stood behind the statutory rate and we will always voice our concern.. We want the Crow rate maintained.
The Conservatives started out wanting the Crow rate to be dismantled. Now they claim that they want the Crow rate to be maintained and that Motion No. 58 in the name of one of their Members is designed to put pressure on the rail companies to give better service.
1 do not know if those Conservatives who claim to be permit book holders are talking as grain shippers; I think the term is "bull shippers". The things they have said did not have a lot to do with the transportation of grain. The only other agricultural commodity involved would be livestock, so I think "bull shippers" would be more appropriate than grain shippers when applied to Members of the Conservative Party.
The change in the Conservative position is phenomenal. Just let us look at the effects of this in western Canada. They claim that Motion No. 58 will ensure that grain companies provide better movement for grain. I say that that is a false contention. The same thing appears in Section 262 of the Railway Act. In the Battlefords-Meadowlake we have not had good movement of grain or good rail transportation for many years.
My constituency contains about 70,000 square miles and not one passenger train moves through that entire section of Canada. There are branch lines going into such places as Meadow Lake where you cannot take a hopper car in. If you rode a hopper car in you could not haul it out because the rail is so light the track would buckle under the weight of a fully loaded car.

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
If Bill C-155, the concoction of Liberals and Conservatives, goes through, it will cost the people who haul to the Meadow Lake delivery point, $1,438,000 more per year than they are paying at the present time.
Look at the situation in the city of North Battleford. I am not referring to the town. It will cost the city $1,155,000 more per year for the delivery point at North Battleford. Battleford, which is often referred to as The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, because there is a town on one side of the river named Battleford and on the north side of the river there is the city of North Battleford, is a delivery point which will cost the producers who haul there each year, $917,000 a year more to haul their grain to the market. We feel that is unfair. Hon. Members criticized the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mr. Waddell) when he said the legislation was a piece of fluff. But the legislation is a piece of fluff. There is no protection for the producers. There are all kinds of written in protection for the rail companies. Motion No. 58, as presented by the Conservative Party, should in fact say at the conclusion that if that performance is not met by the rail companies in Canada, they do not get any return; their investment is guaranteed by the Government of Canada. If they do not provide the service, they can suffer the loss. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that at certain times the rail companies do give good service, but we are dependent upon their inclination as to whether they want to move the grain from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency or whether they do not want to move the grain. It is not working, Mr. Speaker. You cannot whitewash the rail companies to the people and farmers in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake who rely on agriculture. They not only know that this legislation is not in their best interests, they also know that the Conservative Party of Canada and the Liberals certainly do not represent their best interests. Otherwise this piece of legislation would not be before Parliament.
If the Conservative Party really wanted to protect the best interests of the farmers, it could have broken this Bill into the three sections, which the New Democratic Party recommended. Because of the complexities of this legislation, we wanted the Bill broken up into three distinct areas: first, an area dealing with the statutory rate for the movement of grain in western Canada; second, a section dealing with the upgrading and improvement of the rail transportation system; and third, a section dealing with the Dominion coal blocks. If the Conservative Party had the best interests of our producers at heart it would have supported us in this intent. The Conservative Party did that when there was a Bill for the oil companies before the House. It let the bells ring for 14 days in the House of Commons, holding Parliament to ransom. Those Hon. Members did it for the oil companies, but they sure will not do it for the farmers of western Canada, Mr. Speaker. They backed down. They know they would do exactly the same thing that the Liberals are doing today.
What motivates that Party to do that? I do not know for sure. Is it the $50,000 a year which CPR gives not only to the Liberal Party, but to the Conservative Party of Canada as
well? Regardless of which of the major political Parties gets elected in Canada, the best interests of CPR are protected.
Talk about how much CN gives the two political Parties. Tell us about the CNR.

Some Tory Members are asking about the CNR. The CNR came about back in the 1920s because of Liberal and Conservative administrations which had allowed a number of rail companies to develop in Canada, which all became bankrupt. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce was about to go under because of the heavy loans it had made to bankrupt rail companies which had received patronage from Liberals and Conservatives. Finally, the Government at that time decided to save the Liberals, Conservatives and the banks of Canada and form one national railway company. As the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) said, "Socialism for the wealthy". When the CNR finally came about, it was at a bit of a disadvantage as a national transportation company, a Crown corporation, because as we all know-at least we all should know-it came into being with a debt in excess of $1 billion.
That is not much in terms of Government spending today, Mr. Speaker, but back in 1923, $1 billion was a lot of money to be handed over to a railway company which was not even expected to succeed. Some people still question whether the CNR has succeeded. I believe is has done amazingly well with the debt load it had when it started out back in the 1920s. That is the story of the CNR, Mr. Speaker. It has never been on as favourable a footing with a government-whether Liberal or Conservative-as Canadian Pacific Railway has.
Before I conclude my remarks I think I should also mention the windfall which has been given to CPR. It was supposed to receive, over its period of existence, some 43 million acres of land and several hundred millions of dollars. In fact, if you take all the benefits which have been given to CPR since its beginning, added on to present day dollars, its entire assets have been paid for by the Canadian people. Of course, it should give good service from time to time. However, I maintain it could have done a little better in terms of taking branch lines, like the one in Meadow Lake, and making sure one could haul a fully loaded hopper car out over that CP line. It should also have made sure that its sidings in such places as Denholm and Brada are sufficient to unload enough boxcars so that the elevators are not plugged for a good portion of the year.
There have been some problems with the movement of grain. I would not want to say it is all because of Canadian Pacific or Canadian National. The root of the problem lies here in this House, Mr. Speaker, with Hon. Members who have an ignorance of the grain transportation system in this country. Hon. Members from the Conservative and Liberal Parties have continually propped up the rail system of grain transportation in this country. So I do not blame the rail companies, Mr. Speaker. I blame the inadequate administration of Conservative and Liberal Governments which have ruled this country since 1867. Hon. Members should not try to lay the blame on the New Democratic Party. They should not
November 3, 1983

try to lay the blame on the producers of western Canada. The blame lies here with inept Governments which have led this country into the state it is in right now.
If this Bill goes through, even with motion No. 58, we will find ourselves in a situation where the farmers of western Canada cannot compete in the international markets. Once that happens we will be working for legislation a few Parliaments from now-
Order.
-asking for help for the farmers of western Canada because they cannot meet the financial obligations which have been placed on them by these Governments over so many years.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to try to clear up a couple of points before I deal with the particular motion. These were points made by two or three former speakers. The Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish), in spite of the fact that the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) challenged him this morning to give proof that the Progressive Conservative Party would bring in this Bill if we were in power, continued that allegation this afternoon. The NDP is pretty devoid of arguments which are sound if it has to dream things up for which it has no proof. The Hon. Member is having a hallucination. In no way would a Progressive Conservative Government ever present this Bill the way it is today. The Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake should accept that. He has no proof that we would do it because no proof exists. The very fact that we have opposed this Bill indicates that we would not bring in this type of legislation. I will not spend any more time on this because it is a hallucination and the people out there will know it.
The Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Demers) said that the Progressive Conservative Party did not know what it stood for, or words to that effect. I believe the people of Canada know where we stand. 1 would just like to reiterate where we stand. We have not waffled at all on this matter. We supported the former Minister of Transport in setting up a commission to study the anomalies which existed for western Canada and try to solve them. We spent $400,000 of the taxpayers' money on a report. The various grain, cattle, hog and processing people spent probably close to $1 million in arriving at a consensus. Then, when Gilson reported that he wanted the money to be divided 81/19 to start with and then gradually reverse it so that eventually the producer got most of the money, we supported that stand. That would have been sensible. As Gilson said, in no way should you give all that money to the railways, but we would give the increased freight to the railways so they could have a paying proposition. The shortfall would go into the pockets of the producers to help pay for the increased freight. That was a sensible arrangement. But then what happened? The Liberals waffled. Then they went 50/50. They said we will give half to the producers and half to the railways. That was not as good as the Gilson report but it was better than nothing. It would have helped to eliminate the
Western Grain Transportation Act anomalies in the cattle, hog and processing industries. It would have given the West half a chance to reach its potential in agriculture.
What happened after that? The Government eliminated the Gilson report, and this number one item was out, no longer could it be discussed. So then came the number two alternative; the 50/50 came up. We generally supported that because some of the money would go into the pockets of the producers who are now on a reduced income. Their income is 25 per cent or 29 per cent lower this year than it was last year, and last year was lower than the year before. As the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has said time and again, where is the producer going to get this money for the increased freight? Well, that shortfall would have done it.
Then the Government changed its mind again. It said it was going to give not only the increased freight rates to the railway, but the shortfall as well. We objected to that and we still object to it. It is not fair at all. It is completely contrary to what Gilson said. It was the very thing Gilson said not to do. In other words, we wasted $400,000 of the people's money. The industry wasted all the money they spent in trying to reach an equitable and sensible solution to this problem. Then Government said Gilson was no longer negotiable, and the 50/50 was no longer negotiable.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vegreville suggested another solution. He said, leave it up to the producers, let them have freedom of choice. That suggestion spread like wildfire across western Canada. That proposal would give each producer the chance to participate in Government, and it would have given the Government the chance to reflect the thinking of the people. But no, the Government would not accept that proposition. It said this is not acceptable, and it would not even include it for discussion. The Government said, "We have to give it whole hog to the railway, all of the shortfall and all of the increased freight rates". So what could this Party do then? Freedom of choice was gone and the Government was not even going to talk about it. Gilson was not negotiable, the 50/50 was not negotiable, the freedom of choice would not be considered, according to the Government. So what did we say? Well, freeze the freight rates. Put a three-year freeze on so the railway will not get those increased freight rates. They would still get the shortfall, the Government said. They could go ahead with their improvements but there would be no increase for the producer. But the NDP Members would not support that. They are the ones who waffled. They wanted to do something else. Under our proposal, at the end of the third year-at which time 1 would hope the PC Party would be in power-we could then do something to reflect the thinking of the people. But no, that was opposed by the Government and the NDP. It was in the interests of the producers of western Canada. It would have given us the opportunity to do something at the end of three years. In the meantime they would not have been stuck with these increased freight rates which they do not have the money to pay for.

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
No wonder, as the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) said this morning, every organization opposes this legislation. We are giving it all to the railways and doing nothing for the producer. We are destroying the potential of our cattle, hogs and processing industry.
During the term of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) we have seen our packing plants move east. We have seen our hog production in the West go down and down and it moved east. Now the Government is going to do the same thing to our cattle industry. No wonder the people in the West are saying we will never have a chance to play our part in building this country.
That is where we stand, Mr. Speaker. We have not waffled a bit. We have stood firmly to help the producer from square one, and he will be there at square "z" if it goes that far.
The Government says that the amendments introduced by the Hon. Member for Kindersiey-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) are just a repetition of the Transport Act and Railway Act. They are not. They put some teeth into this Bill. They put the Administrator in the place of the shipper. The shipper does not have money to pay for litigation. Lawyers are expensive these days, they cost hundreds of dollars. So what did we say? We will take the part of the producer. The Administrator will become the shipper and he will fight the case in court. The benefits will accrue to all producers. Let the Liberals and the NDP put that in their pipe and smoke it. All the benefits would accrue to all the producers in western Canada. We have not waffled, Mr. Speaker. We have stood for the producer, we stand now for the producer, and we will do so until the very end.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I join my colleagues in debating the closing stages of what has been a long, protracted and bitter debate over one of the most important changes to take place in western Canada possibly since Confederation. That, of course, is the whole question of the transportation system and where we go in terms not only of how it impacts on the grain farmer but also how the transportation system in western Canada impacts on the cattle producer, the coal, potash, sulphur and lumber industries and all of the commodities that are exported out of western Canada, and consequently how that impacts on the rest of Canada. Of course, as we all know, the impact will be substantial.
From a western point of view, it is certaintly with a good deal of sadness that we arrive at the voting stage on a Bill to which we on the Conservative side of the House have been opposed fairly substantially since it was first brought in. Previous speakers have indicated our feelings about where we as a Party would have liked to have gone in terms of the concept of this legislation, but the Bill itself has never been acceptable to our Party. In fact, the legislation itself is not acceptable to western Canada, the area in which it will have the greatest impact.
The various organizations that have come before the Standing Committee on Agriculture have indicated to Government and Opposition Members alike their concern for the legislation. Those concerns are virtually unanimous. At this stage of the legislation, the opposition to the legislation is almost unanimous in western Canada.
All of the grain companies in western Canada, including the pools, have grave concerns with and are very worried about the legislation. The United Grain Growers, for example, another very large grain company in western Canada, is against the legislation. The commodity groups are against the legislation. In fact, many commodity groups tell us they would sooner not see the Bill passed at all. Livestock interests are against the legislation. Truckers are not happy with the legislation. The railways, while they will obviously get more money, are not happy with the legislation. Individual farm groups are not happy with the legislation. Most Hon. Members of the House receive very few letters written by people who in any way at all congratulate the Government for what it is doing.
When the Government flies in the face of that kind of opposition, Mr. Speaker, there must be a substantial fall-out, not only politically for the Party but also for the country itself. We are getting this legislation that we do not want rammed down our throats through closure. The changes that will have to be made to this legislation because it is so unpalatable could very well be substantial and could take a number of years to bring about.
There is no question in the minds of any Hon. Members, except perhaps a few Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party, that Canada needs a better and more efficient grain handling system. There is no question at all about that, Mr. Speaker, because, as we look into the future, we know that the life blood of the country will flow as a result of the exports that are generated primarily in western Canada. We all know that those exports consist basically of raw materials and hopefully at some stage will include processed materials. Initially those exports include raw materials like grain, oilseeds, coal, potash, lumber, sulphur, etc. We do need a better system. We do not have that system at the present time.
The crux of the debate, Mr. Speaker, is surely the kind of system into which we evolve and whether that system treats all areas of interest on an equal basis. In effect, we do not need to have distortions. This is the key question that we have tried to work around throughout the entire debate. How can we best serve not only western Canadian interests but how can we best serve Canadian interests as a whole with a minimum of distortion taking place?
Many people in the country feel that a small step could have been made if we had listened more closely to the recommendations of the Gilson report. A number of Canadians, and probably a number of Members of the House of Commons, have agreed that even if we had taken more seriously the Pepin proposal of method of payment, which was 50 per cent to the railways and 50 per cent to the producers, we would have taken another more positive step down the road to some kind of fairness and equity. What we will have is something that
November 3, 1983

could only be described as a totally botched piece of legislation that satisfies no one because it will be implemented for all of the wrong reasons.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. You were in the Chair when I spoke this morning on Motion No. 58. At that time, four Conservative Members drew to your attention, Mr. Speaker, by points of order, that I was not being relevant even though I was speaking on Motion No. 58. I have listened to the Hon. Member for five minutes now. Not once has he addressed himself to Motion No. 58. I enjoy listening to the Hon. Member because he makes good sense, but 1 think he should save that speech for third reading since it would be more relevant to third reading than it is to Motion No. 58.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, who is a good friend of mine, knows that Motion No. 58 is so broad that a number of topics may be debated. I suggest to him that my train of thought is very relevant to the debate on Motion No. 58 and to what other Members of the House have been talking about.
1 was basically indicating, Mr. Speaker, that in working toward the answer to the question of where we will go, we have come up with the worst possible piece of legislation. As has been mentioned before by a previous speaker, Hon. Members of the Conservative Party have indicated the general position that we would like to take.
The general position taken by the Conservative Party has been stated many times and is basically that the Conservative Party believes that the producer payment in the context of the Bill should be withheld for the next three years. There are three reasons for that position. First, the railways will receive enough money so that over the next three years or so the very necessary rebuilding program will in fact take place. We are assured of that. We feel comfortable that that will be the case. Capacity will not be cut back or curtailed because of a lack of funds.
As the Government has indicated, there will be a committee formed to study the method of payment. That committee will look basically at two methods of payment, one being the Alberta method and the other being the Manitoba Farm Bureau method, and hopefully some kind of equity can be introduced through that study. There is some uncertainty surrounding the method of payment.
Another reason for the position taken by the Conservative Party, Mr. Speaker, is that the farmer himself does not feel that he can pay that amount at the present time.
