Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that 1 have only a minute and a half left. 1 would urge the Hon. Member to listen to what 1 am saying. What I am trying to describe is the general direction taken in the last few months not only by the House of Commons and the country itself but particularly by the Conservative Party in terms of this particular debate.
If I could be allowed, I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that the farmers themselves on the Prairies do not feel they should be paying any more money. When you look at the cash flow charts or sheets which the farmers produce, you find the highest cost they have is interest at the present time. So they feel, and 1 think rightly so, that there should not be an additional burden at this time. If you take those three elements, the uncertainty, the fact there is going to be a revision, the fact that the farmers do not feel that they should pay, there is every reason to wait until after this crucial review of the method of payment is over before payment should start. That is the direction we should be taking in the House of Commons. It is logical, it is rational, and it makes common sense to most producers in this country, and after that period of time, after the three years are up, we can decide with the producers in this country, and after that period of time, after the three years are up, we can decide with the producers and their organizations the direction in which the grain handling industry should proceed.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta). He put on the record a great speech on behalf of his constituents and the people of western Canada. The Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) moved Motion No. 58. This motion is one the Government ought to consider seriously. It puts in place in this Bill the opportunity for the producer to have the benefit of having the railways deliver his grain. If the railways do not, the producer within these number of sections of Motion No. 58 has the ability to question that railway or railways and, through the Administrator, to take the railways to task if the producer feels he has lost money in any way as a result of the way the railways acted. This has always been a concern of mine. In this Bill we have very little in the way of being able to take the railways to task if they do not perform in the way we think they should perform given the subsidy that is being put forward. This motion which takes the good wording from the National Transportation Act and adds to it the shipper, adds to it the ability of the Grain Transport co-ordinator to act on behalf of the shipper in the courts. It makes eminent good sense and should be in the Bill.
We all know it is very difficult for an individual to go before the courts and discuss his case. Why is it difficult? Because in today's system it often costs a lot of money to do that. Very few farmers at the far end of a branch line have the ability to take a railway to task if it does not provide the service. In this motion which is being proposed, the farmer could complain to

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act the Grain Transport Administrator and he could act on the farmer's behalf and take the railway to task either through the Canadian Transport Commission or, 1 suspect, even as far as to the courts and say that the railways are not providing the service they ought to be providing under this legislation. That is why this motion is being proposed. The intention of putting this motion in the Bill is to give farmers in western Canada the opportunity to take the railways to task if they do not provide service.
It costs farmers a lot of money to have the railroads take those very efficient and huge locomotives and run them down branch lines. Neither company has ever proposed building a small locomotive capable of pulling four or five cars down a branch line. They run those huge heavy machines down branch lines and immediately the cost of the maintenance of the branch lines goes up. If in western Canada they had machines built to deliver cars to the mainlines in an efficient manner with very little expenditure attached, I am sure efficiency would go up tremendously. It would seem to me that that would be an interesting concept to look at. I believe Mr. Justice Hall in his report suggested a similar concept to that through the prairie rail authority. That suggestion did not go very far. It is not even looked at in this Bill. There is nothing in this Bill that says the railways need to provide an efficient service to the farmer to move his grain. Yet we are providing over $600 million a year, and over the next three years we are providing over $1 billion to the railroads. We have very little in this Bill to compel the railways to do anything as far as the producers of grain are concerned.
What does the Government say? What is the Government going to do to protect the producer? The Government has brought something forward called a safety net. It is a good idea. It is good protection. In fact, that is what the Crow rate was to the farmer. He would never pay more than one-half a cent per tonne mile. The new idea comes forward that the farmer would pay 4 per cent this year on an increasing rate to 10 per cent in 1988. That is the least he would pay to move his grain. But here is the catch. The catch is that it is an average of six grains moved. When you add up those six grains: rye, wheat, rapeseed, flax, barley and oats, it does not take much calculation to figure out that it would be impossible in five years, given that present grain prices stay reasonably the same, for any prairie farmer to ship barley or oats into the export market. Why do 1 say that? Look at the present prices-$9 approximately for canola, it is called rapeseed in the Bill; I am not sure of the price of rye, but it is about $2.84 a bushel; flax is in the neighbourhood of $8 per bushel; wheat by the end of this year will probably be in the neighbourhood of $6 a bushel; and then you come to oats and barley, barley being $2.30 a bushel and oats about $ 1.40.
When you average all of those together and besides put in the calculation for the number of tonnes moved to port, you will find that the average will probably be based at a little higher than the price of wheat. That means that in today's market, if this safety net is in place, the farmer would pay approximately 60 cents a bushel to move his oats and barley to
market. Given that price, it would be impossible for him to even take them out of his bin.
This safety net does not protect the farmers in western Canada who produce feed grains. It is only a proper safety net for those grains that are at the top of the price scale, namely wheat, rapeseed and flax. In the northern parts of our prairie Provinces there are very few farms capable of producing those grains. 1 suggest that if this is the answer the Government is proposing, it ought to take a very serious look at it.
This Bill as presented to us now under closure of debate needs substantial amendment or else the farmers' ability to pay to move grain to ports will be severely damaged. If we look at the desperate situation of most farmers today, we find they simply cannot, given present prices and cost of production, produce and move grain to export markets in the next few years if we do not have the freeze on the transportation of grain or if we do not have a proper safety net.
As the Members have said previously, if at least the money were paid to the producer he would have a chance to get his grain into the domestic market from the northern parts of the Provinces, to the feedlots, to the manufacturers of feed or food on the Prairies, he would have the money in his hands to transport by either rail or truck to those markets. But he does not even have that under this system. This Bill without the motion we are now debating, Motion No. 58, does not provide any protection to the producer at all. The Bill as it stands now without Motion No. 58 provides no protection to producers; it is a beautiful Bill for the railroads. They will be obtaining a substantial subsidy from Canadian taxpayers. If this Bill is not amended, western grain producers will be placed in serious jeopardy. If the amendments about which 1 have talked are not passed later tonight, there will be nothing in the legislation to assist livestock farmers, given the hurt which will result from the subsidy going directly to the railroads.
I have suggested that if the Government had not accepted the freeze, if it did not come forward with an adequate safety net it ought to have used the agricultural adjustment fund suggested by Mr. Gilson in his report. That $204 million, which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) says is still in the envelope, could be used to assist prairie livestock farmers until the review process is completed. This is just a last-minute desperate plea. We should not have to make such a plea to the Government. It ought to accept eminently sensible amendments which this Party has put forward in an attempt to improve the Bill, but that does not seem to be what the Government is intending. After this Bill is passed there is nothing in the way of the Government to prevent it from taking that agricultural adjustment fund, moneys which are supposedly in the envelope, to attempt to assist livestock farmers until we can put some reasonable sense in the legislation after the review process.
At present we are talking about Motion No. 58. Our Party has put forward many amendments which would improve the Bill; even the New Democratic Party has put forward one or
November 3, 1983

two amendments which would make it somewhat better. When we vote on the motions tonight, I ask Government Members to consider a number of them-and I am not referring to all of them-which will make the Bill even better, given that they have not accepted some of the very important amendments which were put forward. 1 hope the Government will do that and will look seriously at Motion No. 58.

Mr. Speaker, in the history of our country there are certain pieces of legislation which stand out as having been directives in terms of creating an economic climate in a given region or on a national basis which have had long-term effects. For example, we had the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald. It was based on the principle that a fledgling country, largely separated by unsettled areas and an area which was getting a rudimentary transportation system, needed a national policy that would create in the heartland of Canada an industrial base which could serve the rest of the country. I do not have to tell Hon. Members what has been the effect of that legislation on the development of Canada's economic structure.
Transportation and land settlement through the Homestead Act have been a vital and integral part of the development of western Canada. It is important that this legislation was always regarded as a legislative framework which allowed western Canada to develop into the agricultural basin it has become. Having said that, it is important to note that the transportation system can in fact be improved. The status quo does not have to remain untouched.
However, when I look at the legislation before us, I have no doubt that it will hurt western Canada. I have no doubt in my mind that it will hurt the farmers I represent. I have no doubt that the farmers in my area will have less ability to determine how they want to conduct their farming operations. I have no doubt that they will have greater difficulty meeting their expenses and costs. I have absolutely no question in my mind that a number of them will not be able to maintain their farming operations as they are today.
I want to show in a very practical way why the proposals of the Government will simply not have the positive impact which it suggests. Motion No. 58 is another attempt to put into place a provision which will avoid what I think is not only a mistake but could have financially disastrous effect on farmers. This point was already begun by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). There is the argument that a 10 per cent safety net is eminently reasonable. According to the Government's argument, 10 per cent of the price of the product is a valid amount of money to charge for the movement of a commidity. In a very practical sense, it has a very determining effect upon the manner of farming in many areas. Let me be very specific as it relates to my riding.
The riding of Provencher, unlike most Prairie ridings which have an east-west elongation, has a north-south elongation. In the southern part of my riding farmers have made tremendous strides in changing to higher return crops, almost always with concomitant higher risks. However, their return per acre has been enhanced by these new crops. For instance, for years it
Western Grain Transportation Act was not regarded as possible in certain parts of my area to grow dry corn. They are now doing it. We were always importing corn from the Iowa area. Now some of it is produced where we live. That is not where the problem is. The problem develops as we go further north and the different crops which can be grown become more limited. Eventually we reach an area where basically it is oats and barley or coarse grains. When we take a look at the weighted average and at the 10 per cent safety net, the weighted average of those crops, for the purpose of discussion today, would be approximately $5 to $6, and a 10 per cent safety net would result in a 50 cent to 60 cent cost be bushel. It is one thing to apply that amount of transportation cost against a grain which receives a relatively high return, but in an area where farmers are largely restricted to growing coarse grains, where barley might be going at $1.65 and oats at $1.90, we can see that the percentage of the cost of transportation rises well beyond 10 per cent because it is the weighted average. Therefore, when we make this plea to the Government today in the last hours before the voting is to be held, it is a very sincere one.
Day after day the Government says that this legislation must be passed because it will create more jobs. 1 am not arguing that it sincerely holds that point of view. However, if that argument is valid, surely the argument should apply and be valid that farmers who are now farming should be able to continue farming. That makes reasonably good sense. 1 can argue with the NDP Members about specifics, they can argue with me; I can argue with the Liberals and they can argue with me. The point I am trying to make is that under these provisions, some people will not be able to farm. I am saying that it might just be impossible. That is true for the parkland area of the Prairies. The Government is reducing the options which the farmers are going to have.
No.

The Hon. Member says no. When he says no, I hope that he understands the Prairies. The fact remains that there is no better expert in this House with regard to the livestock industry than the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave). I refer not only to his expertise but also his experience. Listen to a gentleman like that and what he says this means to the livestock industry. Members do not have to listen to me. They should listen to him.
When that Hon. Member speaks in the House about the livestock industry and the effect this legislation will have on it, he is not doing that simply from a self interest. If there is any plea I make to the House, it is that the Government look at some of the amendments and consider them seriously. If it is sincere about wanting to create jobs, by the same token this Bill should not reduce the ability to farm or restrict the ability of livestock producers to survive.
I have not had a chance to touch on other areas such as poultry. However, at 6 o'clock today when Government Members stand up, I ask them to consider that many of these

November 3, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act amendments are not Conservative amendments. The only way that farmers will be able to survive in parts of the Prairies is if the Government accepts these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to Motion No. 58. This motion cannot be considered a substantive motion because it is already in the National Transportation Act and the Railway Act. However, the fact that it is transferred to this Act may have some value. Consequently, we cannot say too much about having it here.
We have a few problems with the Bill. One is the designation of the Administrator as a shipper. Within the last year or so, the National Farmers Union took the railways to court. The case was thrown out. The court said the farmer could not be considered a shipper because the shipper was the Canadian Wheat Board.
In this Bill we have the definition of a shipper. It does not go with this amendment. This Bill is badly enough worded without creating further problems, such as the definition of a shipper. That will not help very much. We will probably accept this amendment. We support it because it may do something to strengthen the position of the farmers.
I very much agree with the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) in his analysis of what happens when you increase the freight. A large portion of the crop grown in my area is barley. It is a fairly major crop. We get 100 bushels to the acre and sell it very quickly in most cases. Therefore, it is a very important crop. If we receive $1.90 a bushel and have to pay 80 cents a bushel to ship it, there is no way that the producers in my area will go on producing barley. Therefore, barley will become less and less available. Who will be most affected?
The barley producers in my area will replace the barley with another crop such as canola, wheat, or flax. Therefore, hog producers in the Province of Quebec who depend on western barley will have to pay higher prices for feed from the United States or pay more for western barley. We will not grow it unless we get approximately $2 a bushel. That is what it costs to grow under almost all circumstances.
The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) mentioned the Gilson report. The Gilson report did play some part in this whole operation. Even though it may have been a very bad part, we have to look at it thoroughly.
At a cost to the Government, and therefore, the taxpayers of Canada, of $400,000, Mr. Gilson regurgitated almost exactly the instructions he was given by the then Minister of Transport. If you look at the terms of reference he was given and his final report in summary form, and it included a lot of pages, you find that they are almost identical. Therefore, he merely regurgitated the instructions he was given at a cost to the taxpayers of $400,000. It ended up being of very little value because it did not change the position the Government had taken previously, obviously because it was the decision of the Government.
As 1 said earlier, the amendment established the Administrator as a shipper. The courts have defined the shipper as the
Canadian Wheat Board. If you take away the responsibility of a shipper from the Board, you weaken the Board. Consequently, it does not make sense.
In the last couple of weeks we have received a number of presentations from numerous farm related groups. Just today the Canadian Wheat Board issued a press release in which it suggests that a motion like Motion No. 58, which attempts to put some teeth into the Bill, does not do that. This motion does not do enough to assure the Board that we in this Parliament should support or pass this Bill.
The advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board identifies three or four areas in the Bill which should be changed before the Bill is passed. The Board states that the rates should reflect the grain producers' ability to pay and to remain competitive in world markets. It should exclude variable rates. It should guarantee branch line rehabilitation. It should eliminate the volume cap and it should not affect the Canadian Wheat Board's power to purchase and transport grain. It affects all those matters. Therefore, the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board suggests that we should stop this Bill right now because if we leave those things it will do harm to the agriculture industry in the West.
There is no group in Canada that better represents the farmers or the grain producers than an elected group of representatives who are the advisers to the Canadian Wheat Board. Mr. Speaker, the Saskatchewan Pool has made an almost identical appeal to this Government to stop this Bill. They say: "The transportation Bill does not contain the amendments we require with respect to safety net, volume caps, producers' share of cost and variable rates". Therefore, we can only conclude that this Bill should be thrown out.
It is very important in these last few hours of debate at report stage of the Bill that we look very carefully at the Bill and know how it is going to affect the grain producers. It is going to affect the grain producers, and the cattle and hog producers, not only in the West, but the hog producers in Ontario because Quebec hog producers will be competing for their feed. When that happens every organization related to agriculture will feel its effect. I assure you that not one Member on the Government side, in fact not one Member in this House, can really put his finger on exactly what the results of this Bill are going to be. We know it is going to be disastrous in certain areas for certain parts of the agricultural industry, such as the grain producers. It is going to eliminate the marginal producer. It is going to change the crop structure and the delivery structure. People who now depend on grain crops from the West are not going to get those grain crops because the producers cannot afford to grow them, let alone ship them. If that happens it will change the basic understanding and the relative relationship between the agriculture and processing industries in Canada. We do not know, and the Government does not know, what is going to happen. We do know that for a major group of people in this country this Bill is going to be a disaster. Western farmers now contribute $6
November 3, 1983

billion in foreign exchange every year. This contribution is going to be affected in a major way by changes in this Bill. They cannot afford to pay the freight rates that are being suggested here, and the safety net will not make any difference.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Motion No. 58. This is a motion proposed by our Party and sponsored by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight).
It is a sad commentary on the makeup of the House of Commons when we look at the legislation that is before us and recognize the impact this is going to have on individual farmers. I am talking about the farmers in western Canada. It is a sad commentary on the makeup of this House of Commons when we find there is not one Member sitting on the Government side who directly represents farmers in western Canada. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) is from Winnipeg-Fort Garry, an urban centre. The Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael) represents ah urban centre. There is not one Member of this House of Commons sitting on the Government side who represents the farmers in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy that the Minister of Transport represents six or seven farmers. I am also happy that he represents the elevator companies. Certainly the legislation that is before the House is favourable to the elevator companies, as we on this side of the House have pointed out in committee time and time again. They were one of the biggest opponents to the freedom of choice payment where the producer, the little farmer, the farmer with 160 acres who is growing the crop, has the choice of deciding whether the money will go to the railroad or whether he gets it, which in turn protects the cattle industry and some of the processing industries in western Canada. Of course, this flew directly in the face of the elevator companies and their self-protection and self-interest.
When the committee travelled across the country, our Members put an awful lot of effort into this. The Opposition has been constantly barraged with press releases and statements by Members on the Government side saying that we are being obstructionist and are acting childishly and foolishly in holding up this Bill and trying to work on it.
During committee stage, 89 amendments were accepted on this very poorly drafted legislation. We have on the paper a further 80. This over-all legislation was so badly drafted that
Western Grain Transportation Act
an unprecedented number of amendments were accepted by the committee which, because of the makeup in numbers, is controlled by the Government.
I submit that Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, through our Members on that committee, were doing an exceptionally fine job in trying to make this Bill acceptable to the farmers in western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, let us not oppose Motion No. 58 because it is presented by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster or because it is presented by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition in this House. Let us look at it and see what it really means. This is a long Bill but all it does is to incorporate Section 262 of the Railway Act. That is exactly what the Government wanted in the motion. We carry it slightly further and give it a little more teeth. We add paragraph 10 which says that the Administrator is deemed to be a shipper under Section 262. That means that because the Administrator is a shipper he is in a stronger position and is able to go to the railroads and force them to move grain at the toll imposed by this Act. All we are saying is that we should give the Administrator more power to act on behalf of those small farmers who need to ship their grain in order to earn a livelihood. We should give him the power to ensure that the tarrifs are correct, through the courts if necessary, and to force the railroads to move the grain. That is fair and it is a protection for the farmers.
Our amendment would provide that the railways must move the grain at the toll imposed by the Act. We would leave the rate structure where it is for three years. I have talked to many farmers at meetings in communities in my constituency such as Lac La Biche which some Hon. Members may never have heard of, and St. Lina, Bonnyville and Iron River. The farmers stated emphatically, and in most cases without opposition, that they are prepared to pay more to ship their grain but they cannot afford it now because their costs have increased so drastically. In some cases they have doubled and tripled. The cost of farm fuel has the federal tax in place, and so does the fertilizer costs because all of these are derived from petroleum products and so the petroleum gas revenue tax is included.

Mr. Speaker, I am not ready to hear an interjection from the Hon. Member opposite. He does not represent the farmers of western Canada and he does not have a sense of what I am talking about.
Farmers are hurting out there. They phone every week to ask how they can hang on. Many of them have loans with the Farm Credit Corporation and with the banks and those institutions are coming down on their backs and threatening foreclosure.
How can we in the House justify putting another burden on the producer when grain prices are at an all-time low? Yet we are proposing another burden for the farmers. The effect of this Bill will be to take S400 million per year from western grain producers and transfer it to the railroads.

Time and time again over the last 18 months 1 have seen the Government give that much money and double that much money to industries in central Canada, in Ontario and Quebec, without a qualm, because it claimed that this would save jobs. It is not saving jobs in western Canada; it is killing the farmers, Mr. Speaker. The Government will rue the day it brought this legislation forward. I implore the Government to institute the three-year freeze and give the farmer a little clout by passing Motion No. 58.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motion No. 58 (Mr. McKnight).

Mr. Speaker, 1 am quite pleased to deal with Motion No. 58 which was moved by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight).

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity of serving on the Special Committee on the resolution of the Crow rate all through the months we were discussing it. 1 want to tell Hon. Members that although I do not have any farms in my constituency, the first time I ran in St. Boniface it included quite a large agricultural sector. In 30 years in the construction industry, 1 built a lot of farms, granaries, silos and storage facilities for people in the grain producing business. I learned a great deal from those producers and I still have contact with producers in and around the city of Winnipeg and throughout Manitoba. 1 feel qualified to speak about what producers have to face in supplying grain to the Canadian Wheat Board, which has its headquarters in Winnipeg.
1 served as Parliamentary Secretary when the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) was Minister of Transport and initiated the Gilson report. That report took into consideration the role and functions of the railways.
The Opposition makes a great deal of the number of amendments proposed in the Transport Committee hearings on the Crow rate. The Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) spoke of the numerous amendments that were proposed and accepted. 1 think it is important to point out that some of those
November 3, 1983

amendments covered such things as the inclusion of the word "reliable" after the words "efficient and proper service". I think that this insignificant amendment occurred three times.
It was evident in the hearings that the Conservative Party wanted the Liberals to pass the Bill so that at the next election they could claim that the Liberals were responsible and that they would have done things differently. They could have pointed to the changes that they had proposed and claimed that the Bill was being foisted on producers by the Liberal Party. The Liberal Party has the interests of the transportation system in Canada at heart, Mr. Speaker.
Members of the NDP had their say at the hearings of the Transport Committee across the country. The Committee heard evidence about the things that the railroads must do and their role in improving the system-to double-track, to build the infrastructure needed to move grain to export. In another context in this House, the moment we talk about a lay-off at the CNR shops in Transcona or the western shops in Winnipeg, the NDP says we cannot do that to railroad workers. Members may wonder why we need the kind of provision to make it obligatory that the railways provide service to the producers. I know that Hon. It is imperative that the Government provide assurance to the producers that there will be modes of transportation.
Government Members from Ontario and Quebec may not realize what is happening out there in industry. Right now Smith Transport is undercutting the trucking industry to the point at which it could drive them into oblivion. 1 think those who understand the industry know there are two plans for providing piggyback service for the producer to market. There is a range of charges for plan one which is very expensive because it calls for more equipment. Plan two is cheaper for the producer because there is less equipment called for. At the present time, Smith Transport, a subsidiary of CPR, is providing plan one service to the producer below the cost of plan two. In other words, they are losing millions. Why are they willing to do that? Because in the process they will drive all the trucking companies into bankruptcy. Once that happens, they have the entire industry to themselves. Once that happens, there is no way we can make it obligatory to provide service.
It is imperative that the Government listen to a very reasonable request for a very vulnerable industry, and make this amendment part of the legislation so the producer will have some security. In 1967 this House passed the Railway Transportation Act. In the debate the Government at that time and the Minister of Transport, I think it was Mr. Pickersgill, conceded that you could not in fairness give a grant to one mode of transportation and not to others. You could not give a grant to the railways and not the trucking industry. With that endless supply of money to the one industry, the competition has absolutely no way of competing. I am asking the Government to reconsider its adamant position on the grant system because it is giving a competitive edge to only one industry.

I declare the motion lost.
The next question is on Motion No. 71. According to the agreement, this division also applies to Motions Nos. 74A, 90, 91, 101, 142, 157A, 167 and 170.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am just curious to know when we will decide on Motions Nos. 40, 49, 78, 134A, 84 and 165B. The reason I ask. Sir, is as follows: a negative vote-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Motion No. 77 is in group C. Motion No. 78, which has just been mentioned, is in group B, and so on. The Hon. Member, if he looks at the motions, will find that every one of these cases has been provided for in the grouping. They have been checked and rechecked, 1 am assured by the Table officers. There appears to be a consensus also among Hon. Members close to me who indicate they have also made the check.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry, Sir. This is one of the difficulties when one is working from two different pieces of paper. I asked before the vote started if we would all be working from the same piece of paper. Let me suggest to you that it is entirely possible that Hon. Members might have voted differently-I do not know. 1 will accept the vote as it is.
You have no choice.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Well, I do have a choice. The Speaker in his original grouping made the suggestion that 1 am now requesting be looked at. The Speaker's grouping originally said that a negative vote on Motion No. 39 necessitated a separate vote on Motion No. 40. 1 am, therefore, not at all sure that Members who voted on the last grouping understood that voting for Motions Nos. 39 and 40 at the same time is the same thing as voting for Motion No. 39, and subsequently having to vote on Motion No. 40.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In the interests of following each other, could the Hon. Member indicate which group these motions are from?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I will, group No. C, which we have just completed voting on. The following situation arises: a negative vote on Motion No. 39, which we have just completed, necessitates a vote on Motion No. 40. A negative vote on Motion No. 48, which we have just completed, necessitates a vote on Motion No. 49. A negative vote on Motion No. 133, which we have just completed, necessitates a vote on Motion No. 134A. A negative vote on Motion No. 83, which we have just completed, necessitates a vote on Motion No. 84. A negative vote on Motion No. 165A, necessitates a vote on Motion No. I65B. Finally, a negative vote on Motion No. 77, necessitates a vote on Motion No. 78. I was wondering if you might go through those now, Sir, in order that we-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member properly raises a point in the interests of getting the record straight. Every one of those motions has been included in other groupings for the vote. None of them have failed to be mentioned individually in the course of the groupings. The point the Hon. Member makes is a very valid point. However, it has been considered in the groupings. There could be a discussion, perhaps, between the officers of the Table, to verify. However, I am informed that each one of these has been considered at some point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, they are.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: I do not see them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of the Hon. Member is extremely well taken. This was the original observation of the Chair. However, the Chair can only observe at this point that every motion has been provided for in the grouping. Reference was made to Motion No. 40. This was referred to very specifically in group C. I believe that for any motion that the Hon. Member cares to mention, the Chair can provide a point at which it has been provided for.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We are all working from the same piece of paper.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This disposes of the motions according to the groupings agreed upon.
There remains Motion No. 174 in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin).
Hon. Members will recall that, on October 3, 1983, the Speaker observed that motions to alter the long title of a Bill are not in order "unless such substantial changes are made to the Bill that would necessitate a change in the title to reflect the content and intent of the Bill". In this regard, 1 would refer Hon. Members to Citation 780(1) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, and also to Erskine May's Nineteenth Edition at page 531.
The Chair is not convinced that the amendments agreed to at report stage necessitate an amendment to the title. Therefore, 1 must rule out of order Motion No. 174 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin).
Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Transport) moves that Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as amended, be concurred in.

Agreed.

Nay.
